newsitem.title: UK: Dlr steady in Europe,mark firm on French poll talk.
newsitem.headline: Dlr steady in Europe,mark firm on French poll talk.

text.p: The dollar made a soft but steady start in morning Europe, under pressure from a firmer mark on its European crosses and nervousness ahead of the weekend's G7 finance ministers' meeting.
Dealers said early trade was dominated by speculation of an imminent announcement of a French snap general election, bolstering the mark against the franc and other European currencies.
The dollar showed little reaction to German March M3 growth of 8.3 percent against fourth quarter 1996, right in line with expectations.
"The French election speculation has given the mark overall strength, the M3 data has just confirmed the neutral interest rate outlook in Germany," said a Japanese bank dealer.
Dollar/mark was trading at 1.7018/23 at 0746 GMT, above an overnight low of 1.70 but below late Friday's 1.7126/36 marks.

Analysts said the French poll uncertainty was also denting optimism on Europe's economic and monetary union (EMU), the risk being that a new government may be less willing to push through austerity measures to meet EMU criteria.
But a poll published Monday showed France's ruling centre-right coalition would win an election if held now.
Mark/French franc was trading at 3.3737/39, just below a session high of 3.3745 francs and well above late Friday's European level of 3.3691/94 francs.
Mark/lira was also higher, clearing its ERM central rate of 990 lire to trade at 992.26/55 at 0758 GMT. It stood at 987.95/8.25 lire late Friday.

Mark strength also saw it push higher against the yen, adding to the early pressure on dollar/mark. Mark/yen was trading at 73.59/61, off an overnight peak of 73.69 yen but still slightly above late Friday's 73.54/58.

The dollar made an easier start against the yen but held steady above 125.00 yen in morning trade. Analysts said caution ahead of the forthcoming weekend's G7 meeting in Washington was likely to keep dollar/yen fairly subdued in the short-term.

"The yen issue of the strong dollar is being linked into the G7 and the risk is for a strongly worded statement, this is keeping things steady and stable for the moment," said Tim Fox, treasury economist at Standard Chartered Bank in London.
The G7 meeting on April 27 comes after a meeting between Japan Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto and U.S. President Bill Clinton on Friday, April 25.
